[TODAY] 100 times Hubble's sky in one shot. 🔭

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched Aug. 30 on a three-month, million-mile trip to its working orbit. On Dec. 7, NASA will unveil its first images in a livestream.

Why it matters: Roman's field of view is at least 100 times larger than Hubble's. Over its lifetime it could measure light from a billion galaxies while probing dark energy, dark matter and planets around other stars.

Reality check: these first images show off what it can do; the big surveys come later. You can even adopt a pixel in one of them.

[TODAY] A two-armed robot just launched to orbit. 🤖

On Nov. 24, Russia's Progress MS-36 cargo ship lifted off from Baikonur, Kazakhstan, toward the International Space Station. Its main cargo, per Russian state news agency TASS, is Teledroid: a two-armed robot torso built to help cosmonauts work outside the station. It can copy a cosmonaut's moves or do some tasks alone.

Also on board, per TASS: 420 kg of water, 261 kg of food and 750 kg of fuel.

Reality check: docking is planned for Nov. 26. The robot then faces about 40 test sessions before any real work outside.

[TODAY] Why did the Sun drag a telescope down? ☀️

Low-orbit satellites skim the top of Earth's atmosphere. That thin air slowly drags them down. NASA's Swift observatory had no engine to fight back.

When the Sun hit its stormy peak in 2024, Earth's atmosphere expanded slightly, adding drag. On Oct. 20 Swift sank to 171 miles (275 km) and its team ended the mission. It burned up over Indonesia on Nov. 4.

Reality check: Swift was built for two years and worked almost 22. A planned rescue ended without an attempt to boost it.

Save this for the next falling-satellite headline.

[TODAY] A plane caught dust from beyond Neptune. ✈️

NASA's ER-2 research jet collected tiny dust grains high in Earth's stratosphere. Scientists at NASA and UCLA traced 12 of them to the Kuiper Belt, the icy region past Neptune.

Inside were minerals that formed when ancient water met dust, water rich in heavier oxygen. NASA calls it the strongest evidence yet for an old reservoir of such ice.

Reality check: the study rests on 12 tiny grains. Meteorites rarely show this signature, a hint that giant planets limited mixing between the outer and inner solar system.

[IMAGINE] Two Mars probes waited a year near Earth. 🔴

What is real: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft launched in November 2025, when Earth and Mars sat on opposite sides of the Sun. Instead of heading out, they looped around a balance point about a million miles from Earth. On Nov. 7 and 9, each swung back past Earth and fired its engine for about 9 minutes, a first for NASA on the way to Mars.

Reality check: they are due at Mars in September 2027 to study how the solar wind strips away its air. One mission is a test, not a new standard.

The speculation: what if Mars launches no longer had to wait for the planets to line up every two years?
